statement.title: D. Product of Binary Decimals
statement.legend:
Let's call a number a binary decimal if it is a positive integer and all digits in its decimal notation are either $0$ or $1$. For example, $1\,010\,111$ is a binary decimal, while $10\,201$ and $787\,788$ are not.

Given a number $n$, you are asked whether or not it is possible to represent $n$ as a product of some (not necessarily distinct) binary decimals.
statement.input_spec:
The first line contains a single integer $t$ ($1 \leq t \leq 5 \cdot 10^4$) — the number of test cases.

The only line of each test case contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \leq n \leq 10^5$).
statement.output_spec:
For each test case, output "YES" (without quotes) if $n$ can be represented as a product of binary decimals, and "NO" (without quotes) otherwise.

You can output "YES" and "NO" in any case (for example, strings "yES", "yes", and "Yes" will be recognized as a positive response).
statement.note:
The first five test cases can be represented as a product of binary decimals as follows:

 $121 = 11 \times 11$.

 $1 = 1$ is already a binary decimal.

 $14\,641 = 11 \times 11 \times 11 \times 11$.

 $12\,221 = 11 \times 11 \times 101$.

 $10\,110 = 10\,110$ is already a binary decimal.

editorial.tutorial:
First, let's make precompute list of all binary decimals at most $10^5$. You can do it in many ways, for example iterating through all numbers up to $10^5$ and checking if each is a binary decimal.

Let's call a number good if it can be represented as the product of binary decimals. For each test case, we will write a simple recursive function. $n$ is good if:

 $n=1$, or

 $\frac{n}{i}$ is good, for some binary decimal $i \gt 1$.

 We can check by hand (or code) that the number of binary decimals is not more than $32$, so the solution should not take too long in practice even without memoization. You can test it locally on all $10^5$ inputs to check. This is enough to solve the problem; see the implementation for more details.
Even if your implementation is slightly too slow, there are not many good numbers; you can simply precompute them all locally and hardcode them to get a solution that works in $\mathcal{O}(1)$.
$\phantom{\text{Here is a long string of text so that there is a horizontal line separating sections.}}$
 For the curious: we will compute an upper bound on the complexity, given by the (rather loose) recurrence $$T(n) \leq 2 T\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{10}\right\rfloor\right) + 4 T\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{100}\right\rfloor\right) + 26 T\left(\left\lfloor\frac{n}{1000}\right\rfloor\right).$$ By the Akra-Bazzi method, $$T(n) \in \mathcal{O}(n^{\log_{10} \alpha}) = \mathcal{O}\left(n^{\log_{10} \left( \frac{2 + \sqrt[3]{395 - 3\sqrt{16881}} + \sqrt[3]{395 + 3\sqrt{16881}}}{3} \right)}\right) \approx \mathcal{O}(n^{0.635})\,,$$ where $\alpha$ is the (unique) real number satisfying $\alpha^3 = 2 \alpha^2 + 4 \alpha + 26$. This is probably fast enough, and this is still a very large overestimate.

A more accurate estimate can be made by picking the solution to $\alpha^5 = 2\alpha^4 + 4\alpha^3 + 8\alpha^2 + 16\alpha+2$, which gives a bound $\mathcal{O}(n^{0.587})$.
